items.prompt: A global application serves mostly cacheable public content and users experience high latency to one Region. Which architecture directly addresses the delivery path?
constraints: Content can be cached safely.
The origin remains in one Region.
The application needs a stable public hostname.

options.text: Use Amazon CloudFront as a distributed edge entry point with an origin and cache behaviors matched to the content.
Add an IAM role to every viewer because IAM roles reduce network distance to the origin.
Use a private hosted zone for internet viewers because private DNS creates edge locations.
Move all content into one larger EC2 instance because edge caching cannot serve public objects.

feedback.Reason: CloudFront serves content from edge locations and reduces viewer distance for cacheable content.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A distribution maps behaviors to origins and caches responses at edge locations. Cacheability, TTLs, request forwarding, and origin capacity still determine the result.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect creates behaviors for static and dynamic paths, enables HTTPS and WAF where needed, and measures edge hit ratio and origin latency.
Details.errorCorrection: IAM roles do not reduce viewer latency, private hosted zones do not serve internet viewers, and a larger origin does not provide distributed delivery.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Edge caching improves latency and origin protection but introduces cache invalidation and request-policy complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Identity roles do not change the physical network distance to the origin.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Private hosted zones are not the public edge delivery service.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Origin size alone does not provide global edge caching.

items.prompt: A product page response varies by a safe `language` query parameter, but the distribution forwards every query string and has a low hit ratio. Which change is appropriate?
constraints: Only the language parameter changes the response.
Other query parameters should not fragment the cache.
The origin still receives required request data.

options.text: Configure a cache policy that includes only the language parameter in the cache key and use an origin request policy for any non-cache-key data the origin needs.
Include every query parameter because a larger cache key always improves hit ratio and security.
Disable HTTPS because encrypted requests cannot be cached by CloudFront.
Use an IAM policy to select which query strings CloudFront caches for each viewer role.

feedback.Reason: The cache key should include only response-varying inputs, while origin forwarding can be configured separately.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudFront cache policies control cache-key components and TTL behavior. Origin request policies control values forwarded to the origin without necessarily fragmenting the cache.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner measures hit ratio, includes only approved variation parameters, and tests that sensitive or irrelevant query strings do not create shared-cache mistakes.
Details.errorCorrection: Every query string can reduce cache efficiency and create variance risk, HTTPS can coexist with caching, and IAM roles do not select cache keys.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A smaller key improves reuse but must not merge responses that genuinely vary by an omitted input.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Including irrelevant parameters fragments the cache and can complicate request handling.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CloudFront supports HTTPS viewer and origin connections with caching.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Cache policy configuration is not selected per viewer IAM role.

items.prompt: The origin needs a device header to select a backend, but the response does not vary by that header. Which CloudFront design avoids needless cache fragmentation?
constraints: The header is required only at the origin.
Viewer requests should share cached responses when safe.
The origin contract is documented.

options.text: Forward the header with an origin request policy without adding it to the cache key unless the response truly varies by it.
Add every origin header to the cache key because forwarding and caching are always the same control.
Put the header in an IAM permission boundary because CloudFront headers are authorization policies.
Disable caching for the entire distribution because one origin header is present.

feedback.Reason: Forwarding data to an origin and varying the cache key are distinct decisions.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Origin request policies define headers, cookies, and query strings sent to the origin. Cache policies define what differentiates cached responses; including unnecessary values lowers reuse.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform team forwards the required header, validates origin behavior, and confirms that responses are safe to share across viewers.
Details.errorCorrection: Forwarding does not imply cache-key inclusion, IAM boundaries do not manipulate HTTP headers, and one dynamic input does not require disabling all caching.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Separating the policies improves cache efficiency but demands proof that omitted cache-key data cannot change the response.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Headers needed by the origin do not necessarily need to fragment the cache.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM permission boundaries are not CloudFront request-header controls.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Caching can remain enabled for responses that do not vary by the header.

items.prompt: An S3 bucket should serve objects only through CloudFront, not by direct public bucket access. Which control supports this boundary?
constraints: The distribution is the intended public entry point.
The bucket should remain private.
The design can update the bucket policy.

options.text: Use CloudFront Origin Access Control and a bucket policy that permits the distribution's service principal for the intended objects.
Make the bucket public because CloudFront cannot read private S3 objects.
Use an S3 gateway endpoint because internet viewers need a private VPC route to the bucket.
Use an IAM user access key embedded in the distribution configuration to read the bucket.

feedback.Reason: Origin Access Control lets CloudFront access a private S3 origin while the bucket policy denies direct public access.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudFront signs origin requests according to the OAC configuration, and the S3 bucket policy grants the distribution service principal the required access. Viewer access remains through CloudFront.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner removes public bucket access, configures the OAC and policy, and tests both distribution retrieval and direct S3 denial.
Details.errorCorrection: Private S3 origins can be used with CloudFront, gateway endpoints are for VPC clients, and embedded access keys are not a distribution credential design.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Origin restriction improves control but makes distribution configuration and bucket policy part of one deployment contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CloudFront supports private S3 origins and the bucket should not be public for this requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A gateway endpoint serves VPC workloads and does not secure a public CloudFront origin.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Long-lived access keys in distribution configuration create unnecessary credential exposure.

items.prompt: Customers may download one private video object for a limited time, and each link should authorize one object. Which CloudFront feature fits?
constraints: The content is delivered through CloudFront.
The authorization is time-limited.
The application can issue links after its own entitlement check.

options.text: Issue a CloudFront signed URL with an expiration and resource restriction after the application confirms the customer's entitlement.
Make the object public and rely on the URL being hard to guess as authorization.
Use an IAM role attached to the viewer's browser because browsers can assume AWS roles directly without a federation flow.
Use a security group rule to expire a URL after a time interval.

feedback.Reason: Signed URLs provide time- and resource-scoped CloudFront access for individual private objects.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The trusted application or signer creates a URL with a policy and signature that CloudFront validates before serving the object. The application remains responsible for deciding who receives it.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service checks entitlement, creates a short-lived URL, and avoids logging or exposing the private signing key.
Details.errorCorrection: Public obscurity is not authorization, browsers need a supported federation path for AWS roles, and security groups do not expire URLs.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Signed URLs are precise for individual resources but require key management, expiry selection, and link-sharing risk controls.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An unpredictable public URL is not a durable authorization control.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Viewer AWS credentials require an explicit federation design and are not the direct CloudFront private-content mechanism here.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups do not control URL expiration or CloudFront signature validation.

items.prompt: A user is entitled to many private objects under one distribution path, and the application wants one authorization artifact rather than signing every URL separately. Which option is appropriate?
constraints: The content is private.
The user accesses multiple objects.
The application can set browser cookies after entitlement validation.

options.text: Use a CloudFront signed cookie with an appropriate policy for the private content set and an explicit expiration.
Use a public cookie value as the authorization because CloudFront cookies are never validated cryptographically.
Use one S3 pre-signed URL and assume it authorizes every CloudFront object in the distribution.
Use an EC2 security group to identify which browser may request the object set.

feedback.Reason: Signed cookies authorize multiple private CloudFront objects under a policy without changing every object URL.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudFront validates signed cookie policy and expiration for requests to private content. The application must issue the cookie only after entitlement validation and protect the signing key.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service sets a short-lived cookie for the approved path, revokes or expires it when needed, and tests that other paths remain unavailable.
Details.errorCorrection: Authorization cookies are signed and validated, an S3 URL is service-specific, and security groups cannot identify browsers.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Signed cookies simplify multi-object access but create browser-session and logout or revocation considerations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CloudFront signed cookies rely on cryptographic validation and should not be public bearer text without a signature.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: One S3 pre-signed URL does not authorize every CloudFront object.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups operate on network sources, not individual browser authorization.

items.prompt: A public application must not transmit session cookies over plaintext HTTP. Which CloudFront viewer setting supports this requirement?
constraints: The application has an ACM certificate in the required Region for the distribution.
HTTP clients should be redirected or rejected.
The origin connection is also configured separately.

options.text: Configure an HTTPS viewer certificate and redirect HTTP to HTTPS or require HTTPS according to the application policy.
Use an S3 bucket policy because S3 policies force all CloudFront viewer connections to TLS.
Allow HTTP because CloudFront encrypts only traffic between the edge and origin.
Use a private hosted zone because private DNS automatically encrypts public viewer traffic.

feedback.Reason: Viewer protocol policy and certificate settings determine whether clients use HTTPS to the CloudFront edge.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudFront can require or redirect viewer HTTP requests to HTTPS using a configured certificate. Viewer-to-edge and edge-to-origin TLS are separate configuration decisions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner deploys the certificate, redirects or rejects HTTP, and tests cookies, redirects, and origin protocol behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: S3 policies do not configure viewer protocol, allowing HTTP exposes cookies, and private DNS is not public viewer encryption.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Redirecting improves compatibility while requiring an extra request; rejecting plaintext is stricter but may affect legacy clients.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Viewer TLS is configured on CloudFront, not by an S3 bucket policy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Encrypting only the origin leg leaves the viewer leg in plaintext.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Private DNS does not encrypt public viewer connections.

items.prompt: A compliance policy forbids obsolete TLS versions for CloudFront viewers. Which setting should be reviewed?
constraints: Client compatibility has been measured.
The distribution has a custom certificate.
The requirement applies to the viewer connection.

options.text: Choose a CloudFront security policy that enforces the approved minimum TLS version and test supported client handshakes.
Change the S3 storage class because TLS policy is stored with the origin object.
Use a network ACL to select the TLS version negotiated by the viewer.
Disable the certificate because certificates prevent CloudFront from enforcing TLS versions.

feedback.Reason: CloudFront security policies define supported TLS versions and ciphers for the viewer connection.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The distribution's viewer certificate and security policy control the edge handshake. The origin's TLS policy is configured separately and may have different requirements.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform owner selects the minimum approved policy, tests clients, and plans an explicit compatibility response for legacy users.
Details.errorCorrection: S3 storage classes do not control TLS, network ACLs do not negotiate TLS versions, and removing the certificate removes HTTPS rather than strengthening it.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Stricter TLS improves security but can exclude clients that need migration planning.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Storage class does not control the CloudFront viewer handshake.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Network ACLs filter network packets and do not select TLS versions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A certificate is required for the HTTPS viewer connection; removing it does not improve TLS policy.

items.prompt: A distribution uses a custom HTTPS hostname and must serve many domains without a dedicated IP requirement. Which certificate and delivery consideration applies?
constraints: Modern clients support SNI.
The certificate covers the alternate domain names.
The team wants a scalable shared TLS endpoint.

options.text: Use a certificate covering the distribution aliases and an SNI-compatible CloudFront viewer configuration, while validating client support.
Use one certificate for an unrelated domain because CloudFront selects the correct certificate from the DNS record alone.
Use a security group to select the certificate by viewer source address.
Use a public hosted zone record without configuring a viewer certificate because DNS provides TLS identity.

feedback.Reason: CloudFront HTTPS requires a certificate that covers the aliases and a viewer configuration compatible with the client population.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The TLS handshake uses the requested hostname and the distribution certificate or security policy. DNS directs clients but does not supply the certificate identity.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform team validates ACM certificate coverage, alternate domain configuration, and legacy client compatibility before rollout.
Details.errorCorrection: An unrelated certificate cannot authenticate the requested hostname, security groups do not choose certificates, and DNS alone does not provide TLS identity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: SNI scales custom HTTPS names efficiently but excludes clients that cannot send SNI, which may require a separate compatibility plan.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The certificate must cover the hostname presented by the viewer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: TLS certificate selection is not based on a security-group source address.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS maps names to endpoints but does not replace the viewer certificate.

items.prompt: A content owner wants CloudFront to serve a catalog only to viewers in approved countries, while user login remains required. Which design is coherent?
constraints: The business accepts coarse geographic filtering.
The application still authenticates users.
Proxy and VPN limitations are documented.

options.text: Use CloudFront geographic restriction as an edge filter and retain application authentication and entitlement checks.
Use geographic restriction as proof of the user's legal identity and remove login.
Use an S3 bucket policy because CloudFront geolocation is evaluated only for S3 origins.
Use a private hosted zone to make geographic restriction accurate for internet viewers.

feedback.Reason: CloudFront geo restriction is a coarse edge location filter and is not a substitute for identity or licensing authorization.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The distribution can allow or deny countries based on viewer location data. Application authentication and entitlement still decide whether an individual user may receive content.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner configures the country set, monitors false blocks, and keeps user authorization in the origin or application layer.
Details.errorCorrection: Geolocation is not legal identity, S3 policies do not configure CloudFront geo restriction, and private DNS is not a public location signal.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Geo filtering reduces unwanted delivery but can misclassify proxy users and should not be the only compliance control.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Viewer location is not proof of a person's legal identity or entitlement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CloudFront applies the geographic restriction at the distribution, independent of the S3 bucket policy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Private DNS does not provide accurate public viewer geolocation.

items.prompt: The same web ACL protects an ALB and a CloudFront distribution, but the request paths and body limits differ. What should the team verify?
constraints: The resources are in their supported WAF scope.
The rules are intended for both resource types.
The team can use separate behaviors or ACLs if needed.

options.text: Verify WAF resource scope, rule compatibility, request-component limits, and whether separate web ACLs or rule scopes better match each entry point.
Assume a rule behaves identically at CloudFront and ALB because WAF always sees the same request components.
Remove WAF from the ALB because CloudFront protection automatically applies to direct ALB requests.
Use an IAM role to translate CloudFront cache policies into ALB WAF rules.

feedback.Reason: WAF behavior and supported request components can differ by associated resource, and direct origin paths remain separate.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudFront and regional resources have different WAF scope and request-processing characteristics. A rule must be tested against each resource path it protects.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security team compares sampled requests and body limits, keeps the direct ALB path protected, and separates policies where one ACL becomes too broad.
Details.errorCorrection: WAF does not guarantee identical resource behavior, CloudFront does not protect a direct ALB bypass, and IAM does not translate WAF policies.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Shared rules reduce duplication but can hide resource-specific assumptions; separate ACLs improve fit at extra policy-management cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The associated resource and WAF scope affect the request context and supported components.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Direct ALB requests can bypass CloudFront and need their own protection.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: IAM roles do not convert CloudFront cache policy into WAF rule logic.

items.prompt: A response varies by a header that is excluded from the cache key, and one viewer can influence another viewer's cached result. What should be corrected?
constraints: The response genuinely varies by the header.
Shared caching is desired for other requests.
The team can change cache and origin request policies.

options.text: Include the response-varying header in the cache key or disable caching for that behavior, and verify that untrusted headers cannot poison shared responses.
Keep the header out of the cache key because fewer cache keys always improve correctness.
Use a security group to prevent one viewer from receiving another viewer's cached object.
Use a DNS TTL of zero because DNS caching controls CloudFront object-cache isolation.

feedback.Reason: Any input that changes a response must either participate in the cache key or be excluded from shared caching.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudFront can reuse a cached response for requests with the same cache key. Omitting a response-varying header can serve the wrong representation or permit cache poisoning.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner documents the response variation, adjusts the policy, and tests attacker-controlled header values against multiple viewer sessions.
Details.errorCorrection: A smaller cache key can be incorrect when the response varies, security groups do not manage object cache isolation, and DNS TTLs do not control CloudFront cache keys.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Correct cache variation may lower hit ratio, but correctness and confidentiality take priority over cache efficiency.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Excluding a response-varying input can return the wrong viewer's representation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security groups do not control CloudFront shared-cache key behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS caching and CloudFront object-cache variation are separate mechanisms.

items.prompt: A response contains user-specific account data and a session cookie. Which CloudFront decision protects confidentiality?
constraints: The response varies by authenticated user.
The origin can mark responses private or non-cacheable.
Public static assets can remain cached.

options.text: Do not share-cache the user-specific response unless the cache key and authorization model are explicitly safe; use private or no-cache behavior and keep static paths separate.
Cache the response for every viewer because HTTPS prevents CloudFront from serving a cached object to another user.
Put the session cookie in a security group because cookies are network-layer credentials.
Use a public S3 origin because public origins cannot cache private user data.

feedback.Reason: Encrypted transport does not make a shared cache safe for user-specific responses.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudFront can cache responses at shared edge locations. User identity or session data must be represented safely in the cache policy or the response must be excluded from shared caching.
Details.scenarioApplication: The application marks account responses private, forwards only required authorization data, and gives static assets a separate cache behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: HTTPS protects transport but not cross-user cache reuse, security groups do not store cookies, and public origin status does not make private data safe.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Avoiding shared cache reduces performance for dynamic data but preserves confidentiality and simplifies authorization reasoning.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: HTTPS does not prevent a shared edge cache from returning the same object to another viewer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Cookies are HTTP request data and are not security-group attributes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A public origin does not make user-specific responses safe to share-cache.

items.prompt: A team needs a lightweight redirect and header normalization at the viewer edge without a full origin invocation. Which capability should be evaluated?
constraints: The logic is short and deterministic.
The function must run at the edge event supported by the service.
Secrets and large state are not required.

options.text: Evaluate CloudFront Functions for supported lightweight viewer-request or viewer-response logic, with the documented runtime and event limits.
Use a Lambda execution role in every viewer browser because edge functions are client-side IAM roles.
Use a VPC route table to execute JavaScript before CloudFront selects a cache behavior.
Use an S3 lifecycle rule because lifecycle transitions can modify HTTP viewer headers.

feedback.Reason: CloudFront Functions are designed for lightweight edge request and response transformations within their supported limits.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A function runs at selected CloudFront events and can change request or response data according to its runtime restrictions. More complex origin-facing logic may require a different edge integration.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner keeps the function stateless and small, tests cache behavior effects, and avoids placing secrets or heavy dependencies in it.
Details.errorCorrection: Viewer browsers do not assume the function role, route tables do not execute JavaScript, and S3 lifecycle rules do not modify viewer headers.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Edge execution reduces origin work but has strict runtime, event, and state limits that must shape the design.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CloudFront Functions run in the service edge, not as browser IAM roles.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Route tables forward packets and do not execute edge code.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 lifecycle actions operate on objects and do not transform CloudFront viewer headers.

items.prompt: A CloudFront distribution should serve a secondary origin when the primary returns configured failure responses. Which feature should be used?
constraints: The secondary origin is independently healthy.
The response codes for failover are defined.
Both origins serve compatible content.

options.text: Configure an origin group with a primary and secondary origin and an explicit failover criteria set, then test both paths.
Add a second cache key because cache keys automatically fail over origins when the first is unhealthy.
Use an IAM deny on the primary because CloudFront origin failover is an identity-policy feature.
Use an S3 lifecycle transition because object lifecycle is the CloudFront origin health mechanism.

feedback.Reason: CloudFront origin groups provide an origin-failover mechanism based on configured failure conditions.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The distribution sends requests to the primary and can retry the secondary when the configured status codes or failure conditions occur. Cache state, compatible content, and secondary capacity remain design concerns.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests a controlled primary failure, checks that the secondary response is safe, and documents restoration behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Cache keys do not implement origin health failover, IAM policies do not select a CloudFront origin, and S3 lifecycle is unrelated.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Origin failover improves continuity but can serve stale or incomplete content if the secondary is not equivalent and healthy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Cache-key variation and origin failover are separate distribution controls.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM deny policies do not control CloudFront origin selection.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Object lifecycle transitions do not perform origin health checks or failover.

items.prompt: The distribution is protected by WAF, but a public custom origin hostname is still known. Which origin control reduces direct bypass?
constraints: Direct origin clients are not required.
CloudFront is the intended public endpoint.
The origin can validate an edge-specific signal or restrict source access.

options.text: Restrict the origin to the intended CloudFront path using supported origin access controls or a verifiable origin request condition, and test direct access denial.
Rely on the custom origin hostname remaining secret because DNS names cannot be discovered.
Use a private hosted zone for the origin name but leave its public address reachable from the internet.
Remove the WAF association because origin restriction makes request inspection unnecessary.

feedback.Reason: CloudFront WAF protection applies only to traffic that traverses the distribution, so the origin needs its own bypass control.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Origin security groups, signed origin requests, or other supported controls can distinguish the intended distribution path. Obscurity of a hostname is not an access boundary.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team attempts direct access from an unauthorized source, confirms rejection, and preserves a controlled deployment or health-check path.
Details.errorCorrection: Public names can be discovered, private DNS does not block internet access to a public address, and origin restriction complements rather than replaces WAF.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Strong origin restriction improves defense in depth but can complicate troubleshooting and emergency operations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A hostname is discoverable and should not be treated as a secret.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Private DNS cannot protect a public origin address from direct internet access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Origin restriction and WAF address different bypass and request-inspection concerns.

items.prompt: A security patch changes a JavaScript bundle that may be cached at edge locations. Which release action makes the new object available under the same path?
constraints: The object path cannot change immediately.
The distribution is deployed.
The team can accept invalidation cost and propagation time.

options.text: Create a targeted CloudFront invalidation for the changed path, then verify the new object and consider versioned filenames for future releases.
Change the IAM role because cached objects are selected by viewer identity permissions.
Delete the origin bucket because CloudFront always retains a cached copy forever.
Change the VPC route table because edge cache invalidation is a private network operation.

feedback.Reason: CloudFront invalidation removes cached paths so subsequent requests can obtain the updated object.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An invalidation targets distribution cache paths and is separate from origin storage and IAM. Versioned object names can reduce repeated invalidation needs for future releases.
Details.scenarioApplication: The release pipeline invalidates only affected paths, verifies the edge response, and records propagation status.
Details.errorCorrection: IAM roles do not select cached objects, deleting the origin is destructive, and VPC routes do not control edge cache contents.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Invalidation supports urgent same-path changes but has cost and propagation considerations; versioned assets improve predictability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Cache invalidation is a distribution operation, not a viewer IAM permission change.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting origin data does not safely purge every cached object and can destroy availability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CloudFront cache invalidation is not controlled by VPC route tables.

items.prompt: A user still receives an old response after the origin was fixed. Which sequence best separates a CloudFront cache issue from an origin issue?
constraints: The distribution behavior and path are known.
The origin returns the new content directly.
The response includes cache headers or edge metadata.

options.text: Compare the direct origin response with the CloudFront response, inspect cache status and TTL headers, verify the behavior policy, and invalidate or version the path if required.
Restart the origin immediately because any stale edge response proves the origin did not update.
Change the viewer IAM role because cached content is selected by identity permissions.
Add a NAT gateway because CloudFront cache hits are caused by private origin routing.

feedback.Reason: CloudFront may legitimately serve a cached response after the origin changes, so edge cache evidence must be checked before changing the origin.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The distribution behavior determines cache policy and TTL, while cache status and response headers show whether the request reached the origin. Invalidation or versioned paths changes the edge state.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator reproduces from an edge client, compares origin and distribution responses, and changes only the cache or release control that explains the stale object.
Details.errorCorrection: Restarting the origin does not purge edge content, IAM roles do not select cache entries, and NAT is unrelated to CloudFront cache freshness.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Evidence-first cache diagnosis avoids unnecessary origin disruption but requires understanding cache headers and distribution deployment state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An old edge response can remain after an origin fix and does not prove the origin is still wrong.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Viewer IAM permissions are not the CloudFront cache selection mechanism.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CloudFront edge caching is not repaired by adding a VPC NAT gateway.
